name: Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare, by mouth)
short: Case reports: seizure in a woman with epilepsy after fennel oil in cakes; breast growth in a baby on fennel tea, reversed; bleeding at surgery after fennel seeds and propolis. Few trial safety data.
text: Seizures (fennel essential oil, not fennel seed, fruit or tea): a case report describes a 38-year-old woman with known epilepsy, well controlled on antiepileptic treatment, who had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure and was unconscious for 45 minutes after eating a number of cakes containing an unknown amount of fennel essential oil; the authors say fennel essential oil can induce seizures. A systematic review of essential oils and epilepsy lists fennel among the oils whose internal use can cause epileptic seizures. These data concern the essential oil; the abstract of the 30-woman period-pain study below describes its product as an essence of fennel fruit and does not say whether it was an essential oil. Oestrogen-like effects in young children: a case report describes a 12-month-old girl who developed breast development (isolated premature thelarche) after being given fennel tea every day for 6 months; after the tea was stopped, the breast development regressed gradually and was normal by the end of a year. The authors note that fennel contains anethole, a phytoestrogen. Another report states that long-term use of fennel preparations, given to children to relieve gas, may cause premature thelarche (its title calls fennel a frequent cause, but the abstract gives no case count). Estragole: fennel contains estragole, which has been described as carcinogenic, and a 2012 review notes that fennel has been called dangerous for babies on this basis while arguing that other substances in fennel decoctions inactivate estragole. An analysis of commercial fennel teas estimated estragole exposure in infants of up to 51 micrograms per kg of body weight per day from teabag teas and noted relatively high levels in some instant teas made for infants; these are exposure estimates, not observed harms. In a Cochrane review of diets for infant colic, a one-week placebo-controlled trial in 93 infants of a combined extract of Foeniculum vulgare, Matricariae recutita and Melissa officinalis reported no adverse effects. Allergy: in 58 people with peach allergy who had symptoms and antibodies to fennel, severe reactions to fennel were significantly associated with severe reactions to peach, and the authors describe fennel allergy as rarely reported; a case report describes rhinitis and asthma at work from fennel seed in an atopic man (exposure at work, not by mouth). In women: in period-pain trials, only three of the trials in one meta-analysis assessed adverse events, and one reported minor adverse events; the 2016 Cochrane review of dietary supplements for period pain found that only four of its 27 studies reported adverse effects in both groups, with no evidence of a difference but data too scanty for conclusions, and that evidence of safety is lacking. In a 30-woman study of drops of an essence of fennel fruit taken by mouth (the abstract gives its strength as 2%), five (16.6%) withdrew because of fennel's odour and one reported a mild increase in menstrual flow. A 2021 systematic review of 7 randomised trials in menopausal women reported no serious adverse events. In a 90-student trial of a fennel extract capsule (named in the abstract only by a product name) for premenstrual symptoms, no side effects were reported. Bleeding: a case report describes excessive bleeding during and after cosmetic brow surgery in a previously healthy person who had eaten fennel seeds and bee propolis beforehand; the authors suggest that eating the two herbs caused it, and the abstract does not separate their effects. A 2025 review reports antiplatelet and anticoagulant effects of fennel in laboratory (in vitro) and in vivo experimental studies and says that potential interactions with cardiovascular drugs need further clinical research; its abstract does not describe an interaction observed in people.
